name: PT Cakra Buana Resources Energi Tbk

frontmatter.title: Cakra Buana Resources Energi: a leveraged bet on an offshore vessel
frontmatter.summary: CBRE bought a pipe-laying vessel with related-party debt and lost money on the rupiah and the vessel's slow start. The rights issue converts vendor debt and adds cash, but the post-rights share count multiplies and the enterprise value we can defend is far below the post-rights claims: the equity is worth a couple of rupiah per post-rights share at most, and nil in the base and bear. The stock is on the Special Monitoring Board, so exit runs through a call auction. SELL.
thesis: At 30 September 2026 the company reported liabilities of IDR2,090.0bn against assets of IDR1,950.0bn, with equity of IDR-144.9bn; the rights issue converts IDR858.6bn of debt but leaves the residual claims larger than any enterprise value our model can produce [S2, S7].

The Hai Long is the business: it cost IDR1,672.3bn and carries a charter estimated at IDR4,300.0bn over its full term, yet nine-month revenue was only IDR140.4bn and the gross result was negative [S2, S13].

With the vessel charged a replacement reserve at its depreciation rate, the perpetuity DCF gives an enterprise value of IDR252.0bn and the life-of-asset DCF IDR205.0bn; both are below the post-rights claims even with both rights legs counted, so the base and bear equity floor at zero and only the bull carries a small positive value [S6, F27].

The rights issue adds 11.8 billion new shares to a post-issue count of 16,337 million, so the old share's claim on the equity is a small fraction of what the pre-issue count implies; the cash leg is counted at full value in our bridge and the answer is still nil [S7, S12].

The market quote is a pre-rights, thin-float price on a stock the exchange has moved to the Special Monitoring Board on the negative-equity criterion, so entry and exit run through a full call auction; it implies a revenue path the model cannot reach even at the top of our growth range [S0, S4, S16].

blocks.text: **Rating SELL, twelve-month target Rp2, -99.4% expected return on the cum-rights quote.** The target is stated per post-rights share, because the rights issue is effective and the post-issue count is the relevant denominator. It should be read against the theoretical ex-rights price of the Rp398 quote, not against the quote itself: with 11.8 billion new shares at the Rp108 exercise price and a post-rights count of 16,337 million, the entitlement is worth roughly half the quote, so the current price embeds the dilution before the shares trade ex-entitlement [S0, S7, S12]. Struck on that ex-rights basis the expected return is still a loss close to the whole of the value — the target is nil in the base and bear cases and a small positive figure in the bull — and struck on the quote it is the -99.4% shown. Both bases are shown because the reader should see the dilution, not because the conclusion changes [S0, S7]. The primary method is a ten-year FCFF DCF at a 12.6% WACC and 4.0% terminal growth; a life-of-asset DCF is carried alongside it so the reader can see the value with and without a terminal tail [S0, S6]. EV/EBITDA on LTM is not a usable cross-check because LTM EBITDA is negative and pre-rights book equity is negative for P/BV; we therefore carry the two DCFs at full weight and quote the forward EBITDA multiple as a sanity check only [S0, S2].

**What changed in this update.** The exchange moved the shares to the Special Monitoring Board on 4 November 2026 under the negative-equity criterion, with notations E and X, and the stock has since hit the auto-rejection floor repeatedly: in a mid-morning print on 5 November it traded at Rp398 with a cumulative transaction value of only IDR0.3bn — an intraday partial-session figure, not the day's full turnover, and we label it as such [S16]. The negative equity is not new — the Q3 summary already carried equity of IDR-144.9bn — so the operating forecasts, the DCF enterprise values and the target are unchanged; this is a market-status update, not a change of view [S2, S16]. What it does change is the exit: a name on the special board trades by full call auction and the tape shows how thin the turnover is. A registry-based free float of about a third of the shares before the issue, diluted further by the conversion, is a material constraint on acting on the call, though it is our judgment that it is binding rather than a measured fact [S0, S3]. The rights issue stays on its published timetable. One press report describes the rights issue as still under OJK evaluation, but the corporate-action calendar puts the effective date at 23 October 2026; we keep the published schedule and flag the discrepancy as unresolved [S3, S16].

This note is a revision after the red team's round-one review. Four corrections reset the valuation. First, the previous DCF added back depreciation of 34.0% of revenue by FY2030E but charged capex of only 7.0%, so the terminal value funded a free vessel replacement; the model now holds the D&A charge near its actual rupiah level and charges a replacement reserve equal to it from FY2031E [S6, F27]. Second, the previous bridge divided post-rights equity by the old share count; the model now divides by the post-rights count of 16,337 million shares [S7, S12]. Third, the FCFF formula applies the tax rate to EBIT, so the old statutory rate booked a credit on a loss; the rate is now zero while pre-tax profit is negative [S6, S2]. Fourth, and the reason the enterprise value is no longer negative, the terminal year is rebuilt as a coherent steady state: the gross margin is carried to the cash economics the nine-month actuals already show less a falling depreciation ratio, G&A is held flat in rupiah, and capex equals D&A, so EBIT and FCFF are positive in the terminal year and the terminal value is no longer a capitalised loss [S2, S6, F27]. Those changes are why the target is a small positive rather than nil before the bull case, and why the sentiment is unchanged.

The variant view is that the market is capitalising the Gunanusa contract as if the vessel were fully utilised and the balance sheet were already repaired. Neither is true yet. The company bought the Hai Long for IDR1,672.3bn in December 2025, financed mostly by a payable to the seller and related-party promissory notes [S6, F27]. That transaction lifted total assets to IDR2,005.2bn at FY2025 and liabilities to IDR2,090.0bn by 30 September 2026, swung equity to IDR-144.9bn and produced a IDR-191.8bn net loss for the nine months to September 2026 [S2, S6, S8]. Revenue rose sharply over the same period on the vessel's first contributions, but cost of revenue of IDR167.1bn exceeded revenue, so the gross result was negative [S2].

The rights issue is the pivot, and it transfers the equity claim. The company is issuing 11.8 billion new shares at Rp108, of which IDR858.6bn is being paid by converting debt owed to the vessel seller and related parties [S7, S9]. The conversion is committed; the cash portion of IDR415.7bn is offered to other shareholders [S11]. Both legs are the same corporate action at the same Rp108 exercise price, and at the theoretical ex-rights price of the current quote the rights are well in the money, so a rational holder subscribes even though our own fundamental value says the post-rights share is worth less; we therefore count both legs in the bridge at full value rather than the conversion alone [S7, S11, S12]. Counting the cash leg makes the answer harder, not easier: it is worth IDR415.7bn to the equity and the target is still nil in the base and bear cases. The post-rights count is 16,337 million shares, so the old share's claim on the group is a small fraction of what the pre-issue count implies [S7, S12].

What moves the value is utilisation and the vessel's replacement economics, not the coal price. The vessel earns under a long-term time charter with PT Gunanusa Utama Fabricators with an estimated value of IDR4,300.0bn; the contract is project-linked, so revenue depends on how many EPCIC campaigns the charterer runs and how much of each the vessel serves [S13, S14]. The year-to-date run-rate is well below the contract's annual average, and the Q2-Q3 sequence shows how lumpy the work is [S2, S10]. Our base case reproduces the nine-month run-rate and a slow ramp; the bull assumes a margin recovery toward the Q1 economics, still below the contract average. Neither case clears the debt stack [S0, S2, S13].

CBRE is PT Cakra Buana Resources Energi Tbk, a Jakarta-based shipping company that began commercial operations in 2016 as a tug-and-barge operator serving coal, construction, heavy-equipment and agricultural cargo [S6]. Its legacy business is time charter, freight charter and ship management: it owns a Supramax bulk carrier and a fleet of tugboats and deck barges, and manages vessels for third parties [S6, F29, F30]. In FY2025 the time-charter segment produced IDR53.3bn of revenue and ship management IDR1.9bn, so the legacy book is almost entirely charter income [S6].

The company changed shape in 2025. It agreed in August 2025 to buy a Pipe Laying and Lifting Vessel, the Hai Long, from Hilong Shipping Holding Limited for IDR1,672.3bn, and took ownership on 19 December 2025 [S6]. The vessel was renamed Gunanusa Hai Long and is marketed as an offshore support asset for subsea pipe installation, heavy lift and EPCIC work [S13]. In late 2025 the company announced a long-term time charter of the vessel to PT Gunanusa Utama Fabricators, a domestic EPCIC contractor working on the Hidayah Phase I project with a consortium that includes Hafar, the RAJA-PTRO affiliate [S14]. The contract covers the vessel's full term and is disclosed with an estimated value of IDR4,300.0bn; the wording is an estimate, the company is described as a subcontractor supporting projects the charterer manages, and no minimum take-or-pay volume is disclosed, so it should not be read as firm backlog [S13, S14].

The strategic logic is diversification away from coal barging. The annual report describes the offshore division as a way to reduce dependence on bulk-coal freight and to add a contracted, dollar-linked revenue stream [S6]. The logic is sound in principle — offshore support contracts are longer and less exposed to coal quotas than barge spot work — but it has been executed with vendor financing and unhedged dollar debt, which is why the balance sheet, not the strategy, now drives the equity [S2, S6].

The legacy fleet is small and old. At end-FY2024 the pre-acquisition fleet comprised a mother vessel and deck barges built in the previous decade [S6]. A barge was sold in February 2025 for a small gain, and the company has not announced replacement tonnage beyond the PLV [S6]. The Supramax has a nominal capacity of 53,000 DWT and earns a freight or time-charter rate depending on the fixture [S6, F29]. The company does not disclose barge volumes or utilisation, so the legacy book can only be tracked through segment revenue and the fleet count [S6].

Customers are concentrated by contract type. The offshore book has effectively a single charterer, Gunanusa, for the PLV; the legacy book serves coal shippers and industrial cargo owners, with a handful of relationships that the annual report does not name in revenue-share terms [S6, S13]. That concentration is the central operating risk: a pause in the Hidayah campaign or a dispute with the charterer hits nearly all of the new revenue line [S14, S15].

The controlling shareholder is PT Omudas Investment Holdco, which held 61.1% before the rights issue, with PT Republik Capital Indonesia as the other substantial holder [S3]. Both have declined to exercise their rights and have transferred the entitlement to a group of creditors and strategic investors, including Hilong Shipping and the consortium around Yafin Tandiono Tan [S3, S7]. The free float is a minority of the shares and the company is followed thinly, so the price is driven by flows and rights-issue mechanics as much as by fundamentals [S0, S3].

Coal barging moves thermal coal from a mine jetty or stockpile to a mother vessel waiting offshore; the barge owner earns a freight rate per tonne that reflects distance, draft, waiting time and the coal cycle. Offshore support vessels serve a different market: they carry pipe, structures, equipment and crews for oil and gas construction, and are hired on day-rate time charters that follow the offshore capex cycle. Both are capital-intensive, and a vessel bought at the top of a cycle can take years to earn its cost back. In Indonesia, dollar-denominated charter income against rupiah costs and dollar debt is a familiar source of earnings volatility.

The legacy business sits in Indonesian domestic bulk shipping. Demand for coal barges follows the volume of coal moving from mine to port, which is set by the national production quota and by the gap between domestic and export prices [S6]. The annual report notes that restrictions on coal and nickel distribution in 2025 reduced cargo availability and fleet utilisation across the sector [S6]. That is the cycle the legacy book is exposed to: not the absolute coal price but the volume and the freight rate, with a fleet that is old enough to need docking and replacement [S6]. The coal deck's Newcastle path of US$137/t and HBA path of US$118/t — the forecast years that actually feed this model, not the out-years — are demand indicators for this book, not direct price drivers, because CBRE buys no coal [deck].

The offshore business sits in the Indonesian EPCIC supply chain. The company's charterer, Gunanusa, is a heavy-engineering and fabrication contractor that works on offshore oil and gas projects in Indonesia and abroad [S13]. The PLV is a specialist asset: it lays pipe and lifts heavy structures, and it is hired when a project needs those capabilities rather than continuously [S13]. The addressable market is therefore the pipeline of Indonesian offshore EPCIC campaigns, including Hidayah Phase I, where the vessel is deployed [S14, S15]. The oil deck's Brent path of US$96.0/bbl is the number that drives our cost line: it sits well above the FY2025 actual bunker price, which is why the model's FY2026E fuel cost is above the last actual and why the forecast carries a conservatism the report should not hide [deck] [S6]. Higher oil and gas investment also supports more EPCIC work, but the vessel's day rate is set by its charter, not by the oil price [S13].

The competitive position is weak on scale. CBRE owns the PLV and a handful of legacy vessels, against regional offshore contractors with larger fleets and against barge operators with more tonnage [S6, S13]. Its advantage is the Indonesian flag and the relationship with Gunanusa, which gives it a place in a domestic campaign that foreign-flagged tonnage cannot serve without cabotage approvals [S13]. That is a real but narrow moat: the asset is specialised, the charterer is a single counterparty, and the contract can be terminated or paused if the project slips [S14]. The company is a challenger in both of its markets, not a price-setter [S6].

The five forces lean against the equity. Buyer power is high because the PLV has a single charterer and the legacy book serves a small number of coal shippers; supplier power is moderate because shipyards, crewing and bunker suppliers are concentrated; the threat of new entrants is moderate in barging and high in offshore support if rates justify newbuildings; substitution is low for pipe-laying but real for barge transport, where trucks and alternative ports compete at the margin; and rivalry is high in both [S6, S13]. The structural risk is the cycle: offshore support rates and asset values have historically peaked when orderbooks were fullest, and a vessel bought near a peak can be worth less than its cost within a few years [S6].

The coal and oil links in the model are deliberately asymmetric. CBRE buys no coal, so the Newcastle benchmark is carried at a zero cost share; coal prices reach the P&L only through barge demand, which sits in the revenue path [S6]. Brent enters through bunker fuel, the largest cash cost line in FY2025 cost of revenue after the depreciation charge, with no fuel-surcharge clause disclosed in the time charters [S6, S13, F3, F9]. That makes fuel a genuine margin exposure and explains why the model's deck-linked Brent adds cost even as the coal price is neutral [S6, deck]. The rupiah is the second macro exposure and it does not reach the forecast through a deck link: the residual dollar payable is a balance-sheet item, so its mark is carried in the scenario and the equity bridge rather than in operating margin [S2, S12].

The record before the acquisition was small and cyclical. Revenue moved from IDR42.7bn in FY2023 to IDR62.2bn in FY2024 and IDR55.2bn in FY2025, while net profit swung from IDR0.9bn to IDR-51.7bn and then IDR-70.4bn [S6]. The FY2025 loss was not an operating collapse alone: the gross margin was 2.7%, G&A was IDR31.8bn, and a further other-expense line took the operating result to IDR-50.4bn [S6]. Finance costs of IDR19.3bn then produced the pre-tax loss of IDR-69.7bn [S6].

The acquisition changed the scale and the risk. Total assets were IDR2,005.2bn at the FY2025 balance sheet and IDR1,950.0bn at 30 September 2026; liabilities were IDR2,090.0bn at the latter date, from a much smaller base a year earlier, because the vessel was capitalised while most of its price remained payable [S2, S6]. The company describes the payable as an obligation to third parties and later converted a large slice of it into equity through the rights issue [S6, S7]. Until that conversion, the balance sheet was a bet that the vessel's charter income would cover the debt service and the rupiah exposure; the nine-month FX loss of IDR117.1bn shows how badly the unhedged dollar liability behaved when the rupiah weakened [S2].

**The data pack is wrong on D&A and on the balance sheet, and we have restated both.** Yahoo's FY2025 D&A of a few billion rupiah is a fraction of the LK's depreciation charge; the notes show IDR10.4bn of depreciation in cost of revenue in FY2025 and IDR14.9bn in FY2024 [S0, S6]. The pack's debt also omits the short-term other payables that financed the PLV, so we restate gross debt to total liabilities of IDR2,090.0bn at 30 September 2026 [S0, S2]. The pack's equity is the June-2026 figure; the Q3 press summary reports IDR-144.9bn [S0, S2]. The Q3 figures are unaudited and come from a single secondary press summary; the primary Q3 LK is not in our archive, so every Q3 attribution below is to that summary and should be treated as provisional until the audited FY2026 accounts [S2, S8]. Those corrections are the difference between a company that looks mildly leveraged and one whose equity is out of the money on our base case.

The 2026 results show the operating leverage and the financing drag at the same time. Q1-2026 revenue was IDR67.3bn and the quarter was profitable as the vessel began earning [S10]. By the year to September, revenue was IDR140.4bn but cost of revenue was IDR167.1bn, producing a gross loss; G&A of IDR13.5bn, finance costs of IDR33.5bn and the FX loss of IDR117.1bn took the net loss to IDR-191.8bn [S2]. The quarter-by-quarter pattern matters: Q2 revenue fell to a fraction of Q1's and Q3 recovered only part of the way, while cost of revenue did not fall with it, so the nine-month gross margin is worse than Q1's and the Q3 margin is the trough of the sequence [S2, S10]. That is why we do not extrapolate the Q1 profit, and why the bear charges the Q3 cost level rather than assuming it was a one-off [S2].

Our forecast anchors on that run-rate. FY2026E revenue of IDR191.9bn, 247.9% growth, is the year-to-date actual plus a Q4 at the Q3 run-rate, with the Hidayah campaign expected to lift the second half [S2, S15]. FY2027E revenue of IDR239.3bn assumes a full year at the Q3 run-rate plus a modest utilisation gain, still well below the contract's annual average implied by IDR4,300.0bn over its full term [S13]. FY2028E-FY2030E grow at 10.0% to 5.0% as the charter fills, with no new vessel and no acquisition [S13].

Margins stay negative at the gross line and improve only with utilisation. The modelled FY2026E gross margin is -19.0%, matching the nine-month actual after the Brent cost link; FY2027E is -10.5%, as fixed vessel depreciation and fixed G&A are spread over more revenue [S2, S6]. The improvement is mechanical, not a price recovery: a revenue lift of the size we forecast contributes roughly the cash contribution margin on the increment, and the bear carries the Q3 cost level instead [S2]. D&A is held near the actual rupiah charge: the PLV's IDR1,672.3bn cost over a twenty-year life is about 52.0% of FY2026E revenue, falling to 34.0% by FY2030E as revenue grows, rather than the rising share a flat ratio would produce [S6, F27]. The LK includes vessel depreciation in cost of revenue, so the gross margin is struck after D&A and the D&A line is an add-back only for EBITDA and FCFF; the two are consistent and there is no double count [S6, F3, F9]. That is why EBITDA of IDR46.2bn coexists with an operating loss of IDR-53.6bn and a net loss of IDR-220.7bn [S0]. The FY2026E net loss also carries the IDR117.1bn FX loss already booked [S2].

Cash flow is better than the P&L because depreciation is non-cash, but it must fund the vessel's replacement. FY2026E FCFF is IDR23.9bn and FY2027E FCFF is IDR32.9bn, after sustaining capex of 5.0%-7.0% of revenue and a working-capital build of 20.0% of revenue [S0, S6]. From FY2031E the capex rate rises to 28.0% of revenue, equal to the long-run D&A ratio, so the vessel is replaced at the rate it depreciates; FY2035E FCFF is therefore IDR11.4bn [S6, F27]. The company pays no dividend and has no history of one, so all cash stays in the business [S0, S6]. The tax rate is zero while pre-tax profit is negative: the statutory rate is 22.0% on positive taxable profit, but the FCFF formula would otherwise book a credit on an operating loss the company cannot use [S6, S2]. The cash-flow forecast does not include the rights proceeds; they are a financing event after the last balance sheet and sit in the valuation bridge [S7].

The balance sheet is the constraint. Gross claims of IDR2,090.0bn at 30 September 2026 compare with total assets of IDR1,950.0bn, and equity is IDR-144.9bn [S2]. The working-capital ratio is set at 20.0% of revenue, the Q1-2026 operating ratio of receivables plus inventory less payables, which is above the FY2025 ratio and below gross receivables alone [S0, S6]. The rights issue converts IDR858.6bn of debt and may raise a cash slug of up to IDR415.7bn, but it also multiplies the share count to 16,337 million shares [S7, S11]. On our base case the post-rights equity is negative at book before the cash portion and thin even with it, and the forecast net loss continues through FY2027E, so there is no internal cash generation to de-lever [S0]. That is the arithmetic the market is being asked to underwrite.

**Earnings-quality flags.** The accruals picture is poor. The nine-month net loss of IDR-191.8bn was driven by an FX loss of IDR117.1bn that is non-cash in the period but real in dollar terms, and operating cash flow is not disclosed in the press summary we use [S2]. The FY2025 cash flow shows operating cash use of IDR-57.1bn against a reported net loss, so the business was not cash-generative before the vessel [S6]. Receivables rose to IDR25.8bn at end-FY2025 from IDR7.8bn a year earlier, and the Q1-2026 balance sheet shows a further jump as the PLV began billing [S0, S6]; that is a collection risk, not necessarily a red flag, but it deserves monitoring [S6]. The related-party dimension is material: the vendor, the promissory-note holders and the rights-issue subscribers overlap, and the conversion price is far below the market price [S7, S13]. That is an optics-class flag, disclosed and approved, not a manipulation finding, but it transfers value from non-subscribing holders to the creditors [S7]. On the IDX regime: the shares moved to the Special Monitoring Board on 4 November 2026 under the negative-equity criterion of the last financial statements, and carry notations E and X [S16]. That is a manipulation-class screen by the method card's default and it is explained: the cause is the balance sheet we have already restated, not a disclosure failure, so we do not auto-pass on it; but full call auction trading is now a permanent feature of the exit until the equity turns positive [S16, S2].

We value CBRE on a ten-year FCFF DCF and a life-of-asset DCF, weighted equally, and we test both against an asset value. The company is a capital-asset business whose value is the discounted charter cash flow net of the capex needed to keep the vessel in class and replace it, so a cash-flow model fits better than an earnings multiple struck on a loss-making year [S6]. The perpetuity DCF carries a replacement reserve at the D&A level so the terminal value cannot assume a free vessel; the terminal year is built as a steady state in which EBIT is positive, capex equals D&A and FCFF is positive, so the terminal value is a capitalised going concern rather than a capitalised loss [S6, F27]. The life DCF stops when the remaining cash flows stop adding value — in this model that is the end of the ten-year horizon, not an early truncation — and carries no terminal tail, so it is the lower bound for an asset whose useful life outruns our forecast [S6, F27]. The DCF is anchored on the nine-month run-rate and the contract's utilisation path, not on the contract's headline value; using the headline as revenue would assume a full charter from the start, which the actuals contradict [S2, S13].

The cost of capital is built bottom-up: a risk-free rate of 7.4%, an equity risk premium of 4.2% plus a country premium of 2.5%, an unlevered beta of 1.00 (the industry default for transport), a debt weight of 53.6% and a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4% [S0]. That gives a cost of equity of 18.6% and a WACC of 12.6%. The debt weight is derived from gross debt over market capitalisation, and because the equity is thin the levered beta is 1.90, well above the unlevered input [S0]. Terminal growth is 4.0%, the house rupiah rate, applied after the charter term [S13].

The perpetuity DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR252.0bn, of which the terminal value is 18.7% — a minority share, so the value rests on the explicit charter period rather than on a perpetuity assumption [S0, S6]. The life-of-asset DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR205.0bn [S0]. Both are below the post-rights claims of about IDR2,090.0bn less the IDR858.6bn conversion and the IDR415.7bn cash leg, so the equity floors at zero in the base and bear cases and only the bull carries value [S0, F27, F41, F49]. The terminal year is the test the previous version failed: EBIT is positive, capex equals D&A at about 28.0% of revenue, and FY2035E FCFF of IDR11.4bn is positive, so the perpetuity no longer inverts the sign of the enterprise value [S6, F27]. One engine limitation works against us: the FY2026E stub is counted from the data pack's June balance-sheet date rather than from the valuation date, which overstates the first-year cash flow by the elapsed half-year; the amount is small relative to the claims and does not change the target [S0].

The rights bridge counts both legs at full probability, because they are one corporate action at one price: the IDR858.6bn conversion is contractually committed by the creditors [S7, F41], and the IDR415.7bn cash leg is an election that a rational holder makes because the rights are in the money at the theoretical ex-rights price of the quote [S11, S12]. Counting both is the generous case for the equity, and the enterprise value still falls short of the claims [S0, F41, F49]. The post-rights share count is 16,337 million shares, the old count grossed up for the subscription ratio; the old share's cum-rights value is derived from that post-rights claim, not from the pre-issue count [S6, S12].

The cross-checks do not work on this name, and we say so rather than dress them up. EV/EBITDA on LTM EBITDA is meaningless because LTM EBITDA is negative [S6]; the peer median EBITDA multiple applied to a negative metric would produce a negative equity value [S0]. P/BV is also unavailable because pre-rights book equity is negative [S2]. We therefore carry the two DCFs at full weight and use the peer multiples only as a sanity check on the bull case: at the peer median, the implied enterprise value on a normalised EBITDA would still sit below the claims unless utilisation reaches the contract average [S0]. The lack of a multiple method is a weakness of the valuation, and the reader should treat the target as a DCF output with a wide error band, not a triangulated number [S0].

**The asset-value cross-check, and what "nil" means.** The target is a floor produced by the methods, not a statement that the enterprise is worthless, and the difference is worth showing explicitly. The only sourced arm's-length transaction is the December-2025 purchase of the vessel at IDR1,672.3bn, struck before the Q3 underutilisation and with a seller that is also a creditor and rights subscriber [S6, S7, F27]. Take that as an asset value, ignore the DCF entirely, and deduct the post-rights claims net of both rights legs: the equity comes out at a small positive number, and divided by the 16,337 million post-rights shares it is a couple of rupiah per share — still of the order of a hundredth of the theoretical ex-rights price of the quote [S0, F27, F41, F49]. The vessel's net book value at end-FY2030E, on the LK's straight-line policy, is lower still and gives a lower figure [S6, F27]. So the most likely value of the equity is a floor value close to zero, and the bull case — where utilisation lifts the enterprise value by enough to clear the claims — is the only path to a positive target [S0]. The annual report discloses no impairment test or second-hand valuation and the Q3 press summary does not give the vessel's carrying value, so we do not put a second-hand premium into the target [S6, S2].

The sensitivity table is flat at zero across the tested WACC and growth range, and nearly flat across the revenue-growth and gross-margin grid. That is not a bug in the grid; it is the debt overhang. A percentage-point move in WACC, a change in terminal growth or a couple of points of gross margin shifts the enterprise value by tens of billions of rupiah, but the equity remains below zero until the enterprise value clears the claims by a wide margin [S0]. The same holds on the one assumption that used to flip the sign of the terminal value: with capex carried at ten, twenty or the modelled replacement level of 28.0% of revenue, terminal EV moves by roughly the capitalised capex difference, and the equity stays at the floor in every case, because the enterprise value is a small fraction of the claims before any of these switches [S0, F27]. We therefore state the answer as insensitive on the target: it is not that capex does not matter, it is that the debt overhang is larger than the whole range the sensitivity can span. The value is a levered option on utilisation, and the scenario table, not the WACC grid, is where the meaningful dispersion sits [S0].

What does today's price imply? The reverse DCF cannot bracket the price at any supported FY2027E growth rate: the engine returns "price not bracketed", which is the quantitative statement that the market value sits beyond the top of our growth range [S0]. That is a single-variable solve with WACC, terminal growth and payout held at our assumptions, so it is an illustration rather than a proof; but the direction is clear. To justify Rp398 cum-rights, the vessel would have to earn close to its contract's annual average from the near term, the rupiah would have to stabilise, and the residual dollar payable would have to be serviced without further dilution [S0, S2, S13]. The actuals do not yet support that path.

Features of the share structure complicate the comparison. First, the rights issue is struck at Rp108, a fraction of the cum-rights quote, and the new shares are several times the existing count, so the theoretical ex-rights price is far below Rp398 [S7, S9]. Our target is per post-rights share; the cum-rights quote and the target are on different bases, and the entitlement does not bridge the gap at our fundamental value [S7]. Second, the free float is small and the price has a history of extreme moves, so the market quote is not a reliable measure of fundamental value on any given day [S0, S4]; since 4 November 2026 the shares trade by full call auction on the Special Monitoring Board, where a printed price at the auto-rejection floor is a limit, not a clearing price [S16]. We prefer to anchor on the cash flow and the balance sheet. The share price itself has a speculative history: it travelled from a low quote to a peak many times higher and back within a year, on a thin float, which is a flow risk rather than a fundamental signal [S4].

The downside risks are balance-sheet and utilisation risks, not coal-price risks. The largest is liquidity: gross claims of IDR2,090.0bn against assets of IDR1,950.0bn, a negative equity position at 30 September 2026, and a rights issue whose cash portion may not be subscribed [S2, S7, S11]. A shortfall in the cash portion would leave the company dependent on further bank or related-party funding, and the residual dollar payable would remain exposed to the rupiah [S2, S7]. Likelihood: medium; impact: high, because it determines whether the equity has any value at all.

The next risk is market access, and it has moved from theoretical to actual. The stock is on the Special Monitoring Board, trades by full call auction, and has hit the auto-rejection floor repeatedly, with the latest session's turnover of IDR0.3bn against a market capitalisation in the trillions [S16, S0]. A holder cannot assume an exit at the quoted price, and a seller into that tape moves the price; the practical consequence is that the SELL is a view to act on before or outside the crowd, not a target to trade to [S16]. Likelihood: certain while the board status persists; impact: high on realised return even when the fundamental call is right.

The next risk is charter concentration. The PLV's revenue depends on a single charterer and a single campaign; a pause, a dispute or a delay in Hidayah Phase I would take revenue back toward the Q2 level [S2, S14, S15]. The company is already in litigation with a ship-management vendor, which it says is paid, and the case shows how quickly vendor relationships can become claims [S12]. Likelihood: medium; impact: high.

A further risk is currency. The vessel payable is denominated in dollars and the company reports in rupiah; the nine-month FX loss of IDR117.1bn is larger than the operating loss before it [S2]. The debt conversion removes IDR858.6bn of the exposure, but the residual is still material relative to equity: the purchase price of IDR1,672.3bn less the converted US dollar amount leaves an unhedged dollar principal, and a move in the rupiah of the size the bear assumes is carried as an other non-operating charge in that case [S2, S12, F27]. The exposure is not one-sided. The charter revenue behind the vessel is dollar-linked, so a weaker rupiah raises the rupiah value of the same dollar charter as well as the rupiah value of the residual payable, and the two partly offset [S6, S13]. We do not model the revenue offset as a driver because the charter day rate is fixed in dollars for its term and the company reports in rupiah, so the translation gain and the translation loss sit in the same line and largely cancel; what remains is the net dollar liability, which is why the mark is a bear-only charge and why we do not claim a symmetric rupiah gain in the bull [S13, S12]. Likelihood: high that the rupiah moves; impact: medium to high depending on the residual balance, and smaller than a one-sided reading would suggest.

A further risk is operational. The vessel is a specialist asset with a finite life and a docking cycle; an off-hire event, a mechanical failure or a certification issue would hit revenue and require capex at the same time [S6]. The legacy barge fleet is old and has been shrinking, so there is no diversified earnings base to absorb a PLV outage [S6]. Likelihood: medium; impact: medium.

The last of the large risks is governance and dilution. The rights issue transfers value to the converting creditors, the controlling holders are not subscribing, and the related-party web around the vendor and the note holders is dense [S3, S7]. A further equity raise, a related-party asset purchase or a debt restructuring on worse terms would each hit the per-share value [S7]. Likelihood: medium; impact: high for non-subscribing holders. The post-rights count of 16,337 million shares against the pre-issue count is the measure of the transfer [S6, S12].

Our scenarios mirror the same drivers. The bear assumes the vessel stays at the Q3 utilisation and cost trough, the Hidayah campaign slips, the rights cash portion is not subscribed and the residual dollar payable is marked at a weaker rupiah; revenue growth runs below base, the gross margin is far worse and docking capex is higher [S2, S12]. The base case is the year-to-date run-rate plus a slow ramp, with the Q3 cost level partly carried into the first forecast year [S2]. The bull assumes the Hidayah and follow-on campaigns keep the vessel busy, the gross margin recovers toward the Q1 economics as fixed costs are absorbed, and the committed debt conversion completes; revenue growth runs above base and the gross margin is better, with lower docking capex [S2, S10]. The probabilities are 25.0% bear, 50.0% base and 25.0% bull, reflecting the wide outcome range and the balance-sheet dependence [S0].

The base and bear cases floor at an equity value of Rp0, because the enterprise value is below the post-rights claims in both; only the bull, at Rp10 per post-rights share, clears them [S0, F27]. That is the central asymmetry: the operating recovery in the bull is real and lifts the enterprise value over the claims, but it requires a gross-margin recovery toward the single best quarter the company has reported and utilisation close to the contract average, and it is the only one of the three cases in which the shareholder is paid at all [S0, S10]. The probability-weighted target of Rp2 is what that asymmetry is worth.

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A quarterly revenue run-rate at or above the contract's annual average, sustained over consecutive quarters, would show that the vessel can earn its keep [S13, S15]. A completed rights issue with the cash portion fully subscribed, and a disclosed plan to repay the residual vendor payable, would remove the liquidity tail and, if it turns reported equity positive, the special-board status with it [S7, S16]. An audited FY2026 result with positive operating cash flow and no further related-party financing would improve the quality of the story [S6]. On the other side, a missed subscription, a covenant breach, a further FX loss, a charter dispute or a further session at the auto-rejection floor would confirm the bear case [S2, S7, S16]. We would revisit the rating on any of these, not on the coal price alone.

Control is concentrated and the related-party map is the main governance issue. PT Omudas Investment Holdco held 61.1% before the rights issue and PT Republik Capital Indonesia held the next block; both declined to exercise their rights and transferred the entitlement to a group of creditors and strategic investors [S3, S7]. The recipients include Hilong Shipping, the vessel seller and a promissory-note holder, and entities associated with Yafin Tandiono Tan and the Saga and Garuda Nusantara vehicles [S3, S7]. After the conversion those parties become shareholders, so the controlling group is being reconstituted through the debt workout rather than through an open-market transaction [S7].

The related-party flows are material. The promissory notes were issued to Hilong, Yafin, Saga and Superkrane, and the conversion price is far below the market price [S7, S13]. The company says the vessel purchase was at a fair value and free of conflict, and the audit committee concurred [S6]. We have no evidence of a manipulation-class issue, but the combination of a related-party purchase, a deep-discount conversion and a controlling holder that does not subscribe is an optics-class flag that warrants a governance discount in the bear case [S6, S7].

The auditor is KAP Kanaka Puradiredja, Suhartono, which issued an unmodified opinion on the FY2025 accounts [S6]. There is no going-concern qualification in the annual report, but the Q3-2026 negative equity and the pending rights issue are subsequent events that the audit opinion did not cover [S2, S6]. The company has no dividend record: it paid nothing in the years covered by the price history and declared none for FY2025 [S0, S6]. Board tenure and independence are disclosed in the annual report, and the president director is Suminto Husin Giman [S6]. The company has a small employee base and an internal audit unit scaled to it, which is typical of a newly listed small cap but raises the execution risk on a transaction of this size [S0, S6].

The exchange status is now part of the governance file, not just the trading file. The Special Monitoring Board placement of 4 November 2026 rests on the negative-equity criterion in the last financial statements, and the E and X notations disclose exactly that [S16]. The remedy is the rights issue and the debt conversion, which is why the transaction matters beyond dilution: if it completes and the residual payable is restructured, the equity can turn positive at the next reporting date and the criterion can lapse; if it does not, the company sits on the special board with a negative-equity tag and no dated path off it [S16, S7]. We treat the board status as an optics-class flag with a hard operational consequence, not as evidence of fabrication [S16].

ESG exposure is mostly operational and reputational. The fleet burns bunker fuel, so fuel efficiency and emissions are the main environmental levers; the annual report describes voyage optimisation and slow steaming as cost and emissions measures [S6]. The offshore business serves oil and gas, which carries transition risk over the long term but not in the forecast period [S6]. Social and safety risks are concentrated in vessel operations and crewing, and the company reports no material incidents in the annual report [S6]. Governance dominates the ESG assessment here: the balance-sheet and related-party issues are the ones that matter for the equity [S7].

The dated catalysts are the rights-issue mechanics and the charter ramp. The ex-date is 3 November 2026, the subscription period runs from 6 November to 12 November and the allotment is on 17 November, after which the debt conversion and any cash proceeds land on the balance sheet [S3]. The board status is a standing catalyst rather than a dated one: the shares stay in full call auction while the last reported equity is negative, and the first test of an exit is the next LK after the conversion [S16]. The next hard data point is the FY2026 audited result in March 2027, which will show the first full year of PLV revenue and whether the audit opinion remains unmodified [S2, S6]. In between, the company's quarterly LK and any Gunanusa work-order announcements are the operating signposts [S15].

The KPIs we monitor are revenue per quarter against the contract's annual average, the gross margin after depreciation, operating cash flow, the residual dollar payable and the rupiah, and the subscription outcome of the rights issue [S2, S7, S13]. We also watch the legacy barge segment for further fleet sales or a collapse in coal freight, and the Navios litigation for any escalation beyond the paid claim [S12, S6]. A sustained revenue run-rate above the contract average, a completed cash raise and positive operating cash flow would force a reassessment; a missed subscription or a fresh FX loss would confirm the bear case [S0, S2].

The valuation is a DCF with a wide error band, not a precise target. The reader should treat Rp2 as the probability-weighted output of three cases in which two floor at nil and one carries a small positive value, once the vessel is charged its replacement cost and the post-rights share count is used [S0]. The gap to Rp398 is the market's bet on a utilisation path far above our forecast and a repaired balance sheet; we do not think the evidence supports it yet [S0, S2].

bear.narrative: Hai Long 106 stays at the Q3-2026 utilisation and cost trough, the Hidayah campaign slips into FY2028, and the residual USD51.5m payable is marked at a 10% weaker rupiah (about Rp94bn). Revenue growth runs 10% below base, the gross margin is 20pp worse every year, other non-operating items carry the FX mark and docking capex is higher. Both rights legs complete in this case as in every case (the bridge is not scenario-specific), so the bear is a pure operating and currency case, not a financing-failure case; a failed subscription would make the bear worse, not better.

bull.narrative: The Hidayah and follow-on EPCI campaigns keep the vessel busy, revenue follows the base path but the gross margin recovers toward the Q1-2026 economics as fixed vessel and crew costs are absorbed, and the committed debt conversion is completed. Revenue growth runs 10% above base (growth is scaled, not shifted, so terminal growth stays near the house 4%), the gross margin is 20pp better every year, and docking capex is lower. Utilisation does not reach the Rp537.5bn contract annual average, so the bull is a margin-recovery case, not a full-charter case.

football.label: DCF to end of life (no terminal value)

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is reconciled exactly to the stated build: nine-month actual revenue of Rp140.45bn [S2] plus a Q4 at the Q3 run-rate of Rp51.49bn (revenue Rp140.45bn less Q1 Rp67.35bn [S10] less the pack's Q2 Rp21.61bn) = Rp191.94bn, which the growth input lands on the base of Rp55.16bn [S0]; the prior 200.0 was an unbuilt rounding and is corrected. FY2027E grows 25% because the Hai Long 106 is under an eight-year, ~Rp4.3tn time charter with Gunanusa [S13] and the Q3 run-rate annualises to about Rp206bn; the base assumes about 45% of the contract's Rp537.5bn annual average, not full utilisation. FY2028E-FY2030E grow 10%, 6% and 5% on contract indexation and fleet utilisation; no new vessel is sourced [S13].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The input is stated at base input costs; the Brent link adds roughly six percentage points of bunker cost in FY2026E because the deck's fuel price sits above the link's base year, so the modelled FY2026E gross margin is about -19%, matching the nine-month actual (revenue Rp140.45bn against cost of revenue Rp167.14bn [S2], unaudited press summary). The path to the terminal is the arithmetic of a fixed depreciation charge, not a price recovery: the nine-month cost of revenue includes about Rp78bn of vessel depreciation, so the cash gross margin at the trough is about +36% of revenue [S2, F9]; with D&A held near Rp100bn the gross margin turns positive once revenue passes roughly Rp280bn. FY2030E +7% at base costs and the 10% long run are therefore cash gross margin near its actual level less a D&A ratio falling from 34% to 28% as revenue grows [S2, S6]. The terminal year is a coherent steady state: EBIT is positive, capex equals D&A and FCFF is positive, so the perpetuity does not capitalise a loss [S6, F27]. The Q3 cost breakdown is not in the archived press summary, so the bear carries a much wider margin instead of assuming the trough is one-off.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Zero: CBRE does not buy or trade coal. Its costs are vessel depreciation, bunker fuel, crew, insurance, repairs, docking and agency fees [S6]; the Newcastle price reaches the P&L only through coal-barging demand, captured in revenue growth.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Set to zero because link1_share is zero; there is no coal-linked cost to pass through. Freight-rate linkage to coal prices is in the revenue path [S6].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Bunker fuel was Rp7.700bn of FY2025 cost of revenue of Rp53.647bn, 14.4% [S6, F3, note 27]; set 14% as the COGS share exposed to Brent. The LK calls fuel the largest cost component [S6].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Zero: time-charter owners bear bunker and the LK discloses no fuel-surcharge clause in the charter contracts [S6, S13]; fuel-price increases are listed as a risk the company manages. Any recovery sits in charter rates, captured in revenue growth.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 G&A of Rp31.79bn was inflated by rights-issue and legal costs on a Rp55.16bn revenue base [S6]; the nine-month 2026 G&A was Rp13.5bn, about Rp18bn annualised [S2]. The input holds that absolute rupiah cost base flat (about Rp17-19bn in every year) rather than growing it with revenue, so the falling ratio is dilution of a sourced fixed cost, not an assumed efficiency gain: 9% on FY2026E revenue of Rp191.9bn is Rp17.3bn, and 5% on FY2035E revenue of Rp356.5bn is Rp17.8bn [S2].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is built from the asset: the Hai Long 106 cost Rp1.672tn [S6, F27] and is depreciated straight-line over a 20-year vessel life (5% a year, the LK's vessel policy) = Rp83.6bn, plus about Rp20bn for the tug-and-barge fleet, docking and right-of-use assets, total ~Rp104bn on revenue of Rp200bn. The charge is fixed in rupiah, so the ratio falls as revenue grows: the FY2026E-FY2030E values are ~Rp104bn divided by each year's revenue, and the long-run 30% holds the charge at Rp95-111bn across FY2031E-FY2035E (about Rp104bn on average) rather than the Rp126bn a flat 34% produced. The pack's FY2025 D&A of Rp7.995bn is wrong: the LK shows Rp10.417bn of depreciation in cost of revenue alone [S6, F9].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: No growth capex: the PLV was bought in December 2025 and capitalised [S6]. FY2026E-FY2030E carry sustaining capex and dry-docking at 5-7% of revenue, rising in FY2029E for the docking cycle; the FY2025 cash capex of Rp26.7bn [S6, F23] included docking and equipment. From FY2031E the rate rises to 28% of revenue, which is the LK's own vessel replacement policy priced in rupiah: 5% a year of the Rp1,672.3bn vessel cost is Rp83.6bn, plus about Rp20bn for the legacy tug-and-barge fleet and docking assets, about Rp104bn, or 28% of FY2035E revenue of Rp356.5bn [S6, F27]. Capex therefore equals D&A in the terminal year instead of the arbitrary 30% the first draft carried, and the terminal year is a coherent steady state rather than one where the company replaces its fleet at a rate its EBITDA cannot fund [S6, F27].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital at end-FY2025 was receivables Rp25.77bn plus inventory Rp6.16bn less payables Rp20.67bn = Rp11.26bn, 20.4% of revenue [S0, S6]. The latest full quarter with the PLV billing on the balance sheet, Q1-2026, shows receivables of Rp72.69bn plus inventory of Rp5.62bn less payables of Rp36.84bn = Rp41.46bn, which is 20.7% of FY2026E revenue (and 15.4% of the annualised Q1 run-rate) [S0]. Set 20% — the Q1 operating ratio, above the FY2025 ratio — with the working-capital build funded as revenue grows; gross receivables alone are not the metric because the vendor and trade payables fund part of the billing.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Zero while pre-tax profit is negative in every forecast year. The statutory rate is 22% on positive taxable profit and the tax line is already pos(pbt) x rate, so no cash tax is paid in FY2026E-FY2035E [S6]. The rate is set to zero rather than 22% because the FCFF line applies the rate to EBIT: with EBIT negative, a 22% rate would book an unsourced tax credit on the loss (about Rp12bn in FY2026E and again in FY2035E) that the company does not receive. No deferred-tax asset or loss carry-forward is valued [S6, S2].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 finance cost of Rp33.48bn [S2] on average gross debt of about Rp1.5tn gives ~3%; FY2025 finance cost of Rp19.28bn on year-end debt of Rp1.12tn gives 1.7% because the vendor payable is largely non-interest-bearing [S6]. Set 4.5% on the modelled gross debt, which includes that payable, to reproduce the run-rate finance charge.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Set 2.0%, a rupiah time-deposit rate; FY2025 financial income was only Rp0.086bn on a small cash balance [S6, F13]. No material interest income is assumed.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: FY2026E zero: the Q3-2026 gross liabilities of Rp2.09tn [S2] already include the bank facilities drawn for the PLV, so opening debt carries them. From FY2027E, Rp25bn a year of amortisation on a post-rights debt stock of about Rp1.2tn, consistent with the rights issue converting Rp858.6bn of debt [S7].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2026E carries the Rp117.13bn foreign-exchange loss already booked in the nine months to September 2026 on the USD vessel payable [S2]; it is a realised loss for the year, not a recurring run-rate. From FY2027E zero, on the assumption that the rights issue cuts the USD exposure and no new FX loss is budgeted; the unhedged residual payable stays a bear-case risk.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: No minorities: the pack and the LK show zero minority interest in every year [S0, S6].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Nil: FY2023-FY2025 paid no dividend [S0, S6], the company is loss-making with negative equity [S2], and the rights-issue proceeds are for working capital and debt conversion [S7]. No board statement or policy sets a distribution.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero in the per-share model: the valuation is presented cum-rights on the 4,538m shares outstanding, with the rights issue as a bridge item. The 11.799bn new shares [S7] are discussed in the report and in the bridge; share_change here would double-count the dilution inside the earnings lines.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House rupiah terminal growth of 4%, below the long-run nominal GDP path; the eight-year Gunanusa charter runs to 2033 [S13], so terminal value sits after the contracted period and carries utilisation risk.

challenges.challenge: The perpetuity DCF applies 4% Gordon growth to a negative FY2035E FCFF of -Rp56.7bn, producing a terminal value of -Rp689.3bn, 108% of an enterprise value of -Rp216.4bn. A negative enterprise value for a going concern with positive FCFF of Rp23.9-42.3bn in FY2026E-FY2030E is an artefact of charging 30%-of-revenue capex against negative EBIT, not a valuation, and half the method weight rests on it. The tv_share of 108% is the tell - the explicit period is positive and the whole negative EV comes from the perpetuity.
challenges.answer: Terminal year rebuilt as a coherent steady state instead of rebutting the challenge. Gross margin now rises to +10% at base input costs (about +7% after the Brent link) on the cash economics the nine-month actuals already show: cost of revenue of Rp167.14bn includes about Rp78bn of vessel depreciation, so the trough cash gross margin is about +36% of revenue and D&A dilutes from 34% to 28% as revenue doubles. G&A is held flat in rupiah (about Rp17-19bn) rather than declining as a ratio. Capex from FY2031E is cut from 30% to 28% of revenue, the LK's own 5%-a-year vessel policy on the Rp1,672.3bn cost plus about Rp20bn of legacy fleet and docking assets, i.e. capex equals D&A. Result: FY2035E EBIT +Rp7.0bn, FCFF +Rp11.4bn, perpetuity EV +Rp252bn with the terminal value 19% of EV (was -Rp216bn with a 108% tv_share). Equity is still below the post-rights claims, so the base and bear floor at zero and the bull alone carries value.

challenges.challenge: The "life-of-asset" DCF ends at FY2030E, five years into the 20-year straight-line life the model itself applies to the Rp1,672.3bn vessel, three years before the eight-year Gunanusa charter ends (FY2033), and carries no residual. At Rp83.6bn a year of vessel depreciation the net book value at end-FY2030E is about Rp1,254bn, so the method assumes the fleet is abandoned for nothing at the exact point its cash flow turns negative under the 30% capex assumption.
challenges.answer: The FY2030E truncation was a consequence of negative FCFF from FY2031E, not a method choice. With the terminal state corrected the life DCF now runs to the end of the ten-year forecast (life_end FY2035E) and its EV rises from Rp130.9bn to Rp205.0bn. The horizon still stops three years after the Gunanusa charter ends because the engine's forecast is ten years; the remaining vessel life is covered by the asset-value cross-check now added to section 4 rather than by an unsourced residual inside the DCF.

challenges.challenge: No asset-value or NAV cross-check is run, although the vessel is the only hard asset and it changed hands at Rp1,672.3bn in December 2025 (F27). Adding even the FY2030E net book value of about Rp1,254bn to the truncated life-DCF EV of Rp130.9bn gives EV of about Rp1,385bn, equity of about +Rp159bn and roughly Rp10 per post-rights share - still 97.5% below the quote, so the SELL survives, but it shows the Rp0 is a floor produced by the method, not the most likely value.
challenges.answer: NAV case now stated explicitly and the target is labelled a floor. Using the Rp1,672.3bn December-2025 purchase as an asset value, ignoring the DCF and deducting post-rights claims net of both rights legs gives a small positive equity value, a couple of rupiah per post-rights share on 16,337m, still about a hundredth of the theoretical ex-rights price. End-FY2030E net book value on the 5% policy is lower and gives a lower figure. Section 4 now says plainly that nil means below the methods' floor, not worthless.

challenges.challenge: The bridge counts the Rp858.6bn debt conversion at x1.0 and the Rp415.7bn cash portion at x0.0, although both are the same rights issue at the same Rp108 exercise price. At the theoretical ex-rights price of the Rp398 quote (about Rp188.6) the rights are 43% in the money, so a rational holder subscribes and the Rp415.7bn is the likely outcome, curing the negative equity. Counting the conversion but not the cash understates post-rights equity by Rp415.7bn and is internally inconsistent.
challenges.answer: Both rights legs now counted at full probability, the same corporate action at the same Rp108 exercise price. At the theoretical ex-rights price of about Rp188.6 the rights are 43% in the money, so subscription is the rational election; the conversion is contractually committed.
